summary: Defines the symmetric key package content type for CMS. It is independent of transport, and CMS can sign, digest, authenticate, or encrypt it.

eli5.summary: This is a standard way to bundle secret keys in a container. Other tools can then lock or sign the container.

subtitle: A standard envelope for handing one or more plaintext symmetric keys, plus their metadata, from one party to another.

tldr.problem: Systems that provision symmetric keys (for example into one-time-password devices) need a common, transport-independent format for the keys and for facts about them, such as who issued the key and how long it is valid.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6031 defines a CMS content type, the symmetric key package, that holds a sequence of keys. Package-level and per-key attributes, taken from the PSKC key container model, carry the metadata. The package is DER encoded.
tldr.outcome: The package itself is not protected. It is meant to be wrapped in a CMS type that signs, digests, authenticates or encrypts it.

today: RFC 6031 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the PSKC model of RFC 6030 and the CMS of RFC 5652.

sections.title: What the Key Package Is For
sections.content:
RFC 6031 defines the symmetric key package content type for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 5652). It is transport independent. CMS can be used to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt it.

The use cases behind the attributes are described in RFC 6030 and are not repeated here. This document also gives ASN.1 definitions of the XML elements and attributes defined in RFC 6030. The structures are written in ASN.1, and the RFC uses the key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY as defined in RFC 2119.
sections.eli5: People who hand out secret keys, for example for little login gadgets, need one agreed way to pack them. This document says how to pack them and label them.

sections.title: The Symmetric Key Package Structure
sections.content:
The content type is used to transfer one or more plaintext symmetric keys from one party to another. A package MAY be encapsulated in one or more CMS protecting content types, and it MUST be encoded with the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). Its object identifier is id-ct-KP-sKeyPackage, which ends in smime(16) ct(1) 25.

A SymmetricKeyPackage has three fields:

  • version: identifies the structure version. For this specification the default, v1, MUST be used.
  • sKeyPkgAttrs: optional attributes that apply to all keys in the package.
  • sKeys: a sequence of OneSymmetricKey values, with at least one.

Each OneSymmetricKey has optional sKeyAttrs (attributes for that one key) and an optional sKey (the key value as an OCTET STRING). It MUST include sKeyAttrs, sKey, or both. An attribute that appears in sKeyPkgAttrs MUST NOT also appear in sKeyAttrs, and the reverse.
sections.eli5: The package is a folder. The cover sheet has notes that apply to every key inside, and each key can also have its own sticky note. A note is never written in both places.

sections.title: PSKC Attributes
sections.content:
Section 3 defines attributes that mirror the ones in the Portable Symmetric Key Container (PSKC) of RFC 6030, to help those using the package with the Dynamic Symmetric Key Provisioning Protocol (RFC 6063). RFC 6030 remains the definitive source for what each attribute means. XML strings become UTF8String, XML date-times become GeneralizedTime, and XML integers become INTEGER or BinaryTime (RFC 6019).

The attributes fall into three groups. Key package attributes describe a device (manufacturer, serial number, model, issue number, device binding, start and expiry dates, user id) or a cryptographic module. They generally appear in sKeyPkgAttrs and are all optional. Key attributes describe one key and generally appear in sKeyAttrs. Key policy attributes constrain a key.

Of everything defined, only the Key Identifier and Algorithm key attributes MUST be included. All others are OPTIONAL. The Key Identifier must keep the same value across later exchanges that refer to the same key.

Date attributes MUST match the canonical dateTime form from XML Schema and MUST NOT specify leap seconds. Enforcement of key dates MAY only happen on the validation server, because some devices such as smart cards have no clock, so systems SHOULD NOT rely on the device to enforce them.
sections.eli5: Each key can carry labels such as who made it, which gadget it belongs to, and when it stops working. Only the key's name and its kind of math are required labels. The rest are optional.

sections.title: Key Policy: Usage and PIN Rules
sections.content:
Key policy attributes include a start date, an expiry date, and a Number of Transactions (the maximum number of times a key can be used; omitted means no limit). The Key Usage attribute limits what a key may do, and the recipient MUST enforce it. A key marked OTP MUST only be used for one-time-password generation, Encrypt only for data encryption, KeyWrap only for key wrapping, and so on.

The PIN Policy attribute attaches rules about a PIN that protects the key: which key holds the PIN, how the PIN is used (Local, Prepend, Append or Algorithmic), the maximum failed attempts, minimum and maximum length, and the PIN encoding. If the usage mode is Local, the device MUST enforce the restrictions. Otherwise they MUST be enforced on the server side.

The Algorithm Parameters attribute describes challenge and response formats for one-time-password and challenge/response algorithms. Encodings are DECIMAL, HEXADECIMAL, ALPHANUMERIC, BASE64 or BINARY, and a Luhn check digit is only valid with DECIMAL.
sections.eli5: Some labels are rules. A key may be allowed only to make login codes, or only to lock things, and a PIN rule can say how short or long the PIN may be and how many wrong tries are allowed.

sections.title: How Raw Key Bytes Are Read
sections.content:
Two parties that receive the same key as an sKey OCTET STRING must use it in exactly the same way. To make that happen, the RFC maps the OCTET STRING onto the notation of two algorithms.

For AES, the first octet of sKey SHALL become key byte index 0 in FIPS 197, and the following octets follow in increasing index order. For Triple-DES, a key bundle has three 64-bit keys (56 key bits and 8 parity bits each). The first octet of sKey SHALL be bits 1 through 8 of Key1 with bit 1 as the most significant bit, and so on, ending with bits 57 through 64 of Key3 (or Key2 for two-key Triple DES, where Key1 and Key3 are equal).

Each case comes with a test vector that an implementation uses to check its parsing and key loading against the published key expansion vectors.
sections.eli5: A key is just a row of bytes, so two people must read the row in the same order. The document says which byte is first, and gives an example key to check you did it right.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
Implementers are strongly encouraged to follow generally accepted principles of secure key management. The key point is that the symmetric key package contents are not protected. The content type is meant to be combined with a security protocol. One option is to use it in place of a PSKC package in RFC 6063 exchanges, in which case the algorithm requirements come from that document. Another is to encapsulate it in a CMS protecting content type.

For IANA, the document uses object identifiers for the CMS content type, the ASN.1 version of the PSKC attributes and the two ASN.1 modules. All of them are registered in an arc delegated by RSADSI to the SMIME Working Group.
sections.eli5: The box of keys has no lock of its own. You must put it inside something locked, like a safe, before it travels.
